title: This ’67 Mini Is a Time-Capsule Driven with Care

body_markdown:
In late fall 2021, I was lucky enough to come across what may have been one of the lowest-mileage, unrestored Mini Coopers for sale. The owner of a local classic car dealership here in Fairfield County, Connecticut, told me that a client of his was downsizing his collection. One of the cars he was selling was a[1967 Austin Mini Cooper](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/austin/mini_cooper/1967/1967-austin-mini_cooper-1275s?id=aCn1I000000DDoqSAG) with 7700 kilometers (4800 miles) on its correct German-market odometer. The car was purchased new in Germany (with all the documents from purchase to support it) in 1967 and later that year was shipped to Boston, where the owner stored it for 55 years.


It was kept clean, started yearly, and driven a few miles. From what I could see, over the years the owner added quick-release knobs for the front grille, an aftermarket tachometer, and an upgraded Smiths temperature gauge. The generator may have been rebuilt at some point. The locking steering column was standard for German Minis and became standard for[all Minis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/one-couples-max-obsession-with-custom-minis/) much later.


Alain Waksenboim


Alain Waksenboim


Alain Waksenboim


Some cool details that are rarely seen are pen markings on the inside of the door hinges, which helped the factory installers easily identify whether they were left- or right-side hinges and whether they were upper or lower placement. Even under the seats, small pieces of the original plastic seat wrap remain. The tires were replaced and are in new condition, but date codes show they are 30 years old.


I agreed to purchase the car, and it was taken out of its long-term storage facility. Unlike most finds of a car of this age, it wasn’t an old, worn barn find. The Mini was in near-showroom condition, with the interior and paint almost mint. What the car did need was to have all the systems checked and gone through.


Alain Waksenboim


Alain Waksenboim

Alain Waksenboim


Alain Waksenboim


I had the hydrostatic suspension pumped up, and it works well. Brakes were checked and I installed a new battery. The fuel system, however, is where the Mini needed most of the work. The original carburetors got a needed rebuild. The fuel tank was always kept nearly empty, which led it to rust and develop pinholes throughout, so I had an original OEM tank installed as well as a fuel sender unit and fuel pump. I had all fluids changed and cracked or worn hoses replaced, and gave the Mini a full tune-up.


It is running great. I have owned and driven other classic Minis, and using this one locally it is amazing to feel what it must have been like to drive an almost-new 1967 Mini Cooper.


This Mini should really be in a museum, but I try to strike a balance of driving the car while being mindful of keeping the mileage low. I am definitely in the camp of believing classic cars should be driven, so I do just that, but sparingly.
